title: Raised with Christ: Putting On the New Self
summary: Because believers have been raised with Christ, they are to set their minds on things above, where Christ is seated. They must put to death sexual immorality, greed, anger, and lies, and put on compassion, kindness, humility, forgiveness, and above all love, letting Christ's peace rule and his word dwell among them. Paul then applies this new life to the household, addressing wives and husbands, children and fathers, and slaves.
story: Chapter 2 said what believers are freed from: empty philosophy, food and calendar rules, and the powers Christ defeated. Chapter 3 says what they are freed for. The hinge is verse 1, which picks up 2:12 and 2:20: since you died with Christ and were raised with him, live like it. The ascetic teaching Paul opposed promised holiness through harsh treatment of the body, and Paul said it had no value against the indulgence of the flesh (2:23). Here he gives the real alternative, a life reshaped from the inside by union with Christ. The chapter moves from heaven, where Christ is seated, to the most ordinary places on earth: the tongue, the table, the marriage, and the workshop.
historical:
The churches Paul addressed were made up of households. Many Christians met in homes (4:15; Philemon 2), and a household included not only a married couple and their children but often slaves, who were a large part of the population of Roman cities. Slavery in the Roman world was not based on race; people became slaves through war, debt, birth, or abandonment as infants. Some slaves held skilled or responsible posts and could hope to be freed; many lived in hard conditions under the full legal power of their masters.

The letter's audience included Gentiles who had once lived by the moral standards of their surrounding culture, in which sexual relations outside marriage, especially for men, were widely accepted. Paul's list of vices in verse 5 would have described common behavior, not rare crimes. The list of peoples in verse 11 reflects the mixed population of Asia Minor: Greeks and Jews, and also barbarians (a Greek term for anyone who did not speak Greek) and Scythians, the nomadic peoples north of the Black Sea whom Greeks regarded as the most uncivilized of all.
cultural:
Instructions for the household were a standard topic in ancient moral writing. Aristotle, in his Politics, discussed household management in terms of three pairs of relationships: master and slave, husband and wife, and father and children, and later philosophers and Jewish writers continued the discussion. Scholars call the New Testament versions household codes (see also Ephesians 5 and 6 and 1 Peter 2 and 3). Colossians follows the same three pairs but changes them in several ways. It addresses wives, children, and slaves directly, as moral persons responsible to the Lord, not merely as property or dependents to be managed. It places duties on husbands, fathers, and masters as well: love, gentleness, fairness. And it grounds every instruction in the Lord.

The clothing language of putting off and putting on runs through the chapter. Changing clothes was a vivid image for a change of identity, and many scholars think it reflects early Christian baptism, in which converts may have removed their old clothes before being baptized and put on new ones afterward. The singing in verse 16 reflects early Christian worship: the psalms of Israel, hymns of praise, and songs prompted by the Spirit.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 4 give the foundation in the language of death, resurrection, and hiddenness: you died, you were raised, your life is hidden with Christ, and it will appear with him. Verses 5 to 17 give the pattern of the new life in two movements, putting off (verses 5 to 11) and putting on (verses 12 to 17). Each movement contains lists, the vices in two groups of five (verses 5 and 8) and the virtues in a group of five (verse 12). The section climaxes with love as the garment over everything, the peace of Christ ruling, the word of Christ dwelling, and everything done in the name of the Lord Jesus with thanks. Verses 18 to 25 begin the household code, which runs into 4:1. Its short commands are carefully paired, and the phrase the Lord recurs again and again, especially in the longest section, which is addressed to slaves.

outline.t: Raised with Christ: set your minds above
Put on the new self, clothed in love
Wives and husbands, children and fathers

doctrines.note: Believers have died with Christ and been raised with him; their life is hidden with Christ in God and will be revealed when he appears (verses 1 to 4). Holiness is not the way to earn this new life but the way to live it out.
Paul calls greed idolatry (verse 5). An idol is not only a statue; it is whatever a person looks to for security and satisfaction in place of God. The desire for more is a form of worship.

The household relationships are reordered in the Lord. Each member receives a calling, and the stronger party in each pair is given duties of love and restraint, not only rights. Christians disagree over how the instructions to wives apply today, as discussed below.

The new self is being renewed in the image of its creator, and in it the old divisions of ethnicity, religion, culture, and social class no longer define people: Christ is all and in all (verses 10 and 11). The church is called to be one body, ruled by Christ's peace.

words.note: Enduo, to put on, as of clothing. Paul says believers have put on the new self (verse 10) and must clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, and over all these, love (verses 12 and 14). The image suggests both something already done (a new identity) and something to be done daily (choosing to wear it).

Nekroo, to put to death. A strong word: Paul does not say manage or reduce but kill the earthly practices. This is not the harsh treatment of the body he rejected in 2:23, but a decisive refusal of sinful desires, grounded in the fact that believers have already died with Christ (verse 3).

Brabeuo, to act as umpire or rule. The word was used of the judge who decides the prize in an athletic contest. Paul asks that the peace of Christ act as umpire in believers' hearts, settling disputes and deciding between competing impulses, because they were called to peace as one body.

christ: The whole chapter depends on the believer's union with Christ. Christ is raised and seated at the right hand of God (verse 1), echoing Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New. The believer's life is hidden with him, and Christ is called your life (verse 4). The new self is renewed in the image of its creator, which recalls 1:15, where Christ is the image of the invisible God: to become new is to become like Christ. Believers forgive as the Lord forgave them (verse 13), let the word of Christ dwell in them, and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. Even slaves are told that it is the Lord Christ they are serving (verse 24). Christ is not only the object of faith but the pattern, the power, and the Lord of every ordinary relationship.

hard.q: How should readers today understand the instructions to wives and to slaves?
hard.a: Two instructions trouble many modern readers. On slavery, Paul does not call for its abolition, and later Christians used such passages to defend it, including in the American South. Defenders of the text point out that Paul addresses slaves as full members of the church with moral dignity, tells masters that they too have a Master in heaven and must treat slaves justly and fairly (4:1), declares that in Christ there is neither slave nor free (verse 11), and elsewhere urges Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother. Many Christians see here the seeds that would eventually undo slavery, though the church took far too long to act on them. On wives, Christians are divided. Complementarians hold that the call for wives to submit to their husbands, paired with the call for husbands to love and not be harsh, reflects a lasting pattern of loving male headship in marriage, though never a license for abuse. Egalitarians hold that it applied the gospel within the household structure of the time, and that its principles (mutual love and service, as in Ephesians 5:21) point toward partnership without a hierarchy of roles. Both sides agree that the instructions reject domination and set every relationship under the lordship of Christ.

questions: What would it look like, practically, to set your mind on things above this week without withdrawing from ordinary life?
Paul calls greed idolatry. Where might the desire for more be functioning as a god in your life?
Verse 23 tells workers to work for the Lord and not for men. How would that change the way you approach tasks nobody sees or thanks you for?
